The house, which had once seemed to me a fortress of immeasurable grandeur, now struck me as merely large; its stony silence no longer held the power to cow my spirit into submission. As I stood in the great hall, under the baleful gaze of a long-dead ancestor’s portrait, I was conscious of a strange new fortitude. The butler, a man whose severe countenance had been the terror of my girlhood, had received me with a stiff inclination of his head and the barest murmur of my name; yet his coldness did not wound, nor did the oppressive quiet of the place chill me. My heart had, in the intervening years, been schooled in sorrows and in joys of a far deeper make than any this house could offer; I had known true hardship and found true affection, and the theatrics of the wealthy seemed but a pale and pitiful show.

“Mr. Alistair is resting,” the butler, Phelps, had informed me, his tone implying that this state should on no account be disturbed. “He did not say at what hour he would be prepared to receive you.”

“I am sure he did not,” I replied, my voice more steady than I might have hoped. “Nevertheless, you would oblige me by sending word that his sister has arrived. He did, after all, summon me.”

Phelps’s thin eyebrows rose a fraction. “As you wish, miss.”

He departed, his shoes making no sound on the marble floor, and left me to my reflections. A younger version of myself would have shrunk into a corner, perching on the edge of a hard-backed chair until bidden to move; she would have quaked at every creak of the floorboards above, dreading the summons that would bring her before her imperious elder brother. But I was that girl no longer. I had travelled two days to answer Alistair’s letter, a missive as brief and commanding as the man himself, and I would not be made to feel like a beggar at the gate.

With a resolve that felt both foreign and exhilarating, I placed my travelling bag upon a velvet settee, an act of sacrilege in my youth, and made my own way to the grand staircase. I knew the path to his chambers; it was a route I had seldom been permitted to take, for his wing of the house was his own private kingdom. I ascended, my hand gliding over the smooth, cool oak of the banister, and found a maidservant hovering anxiously on the landing.

“He is awake,” she whispered, wringing her hands. “He asked for water, miss. He is in a difficult temper.”

“He is always in a difficult temper,” I said, and was surprised at the lack of bitterness in my own words; it was a simple statement of fact, like observing that the sky is blue. I continued past her and tapped softly on the door before opening it and stepping inside.

There was the familiar scent of leather and old paper, now mingled with the sour odour of sickness. The great mahogany desk was as cluttered as ever, the shelves groaned with books, but a fire burned low in the hearth, though the day was mild. And there, in a brocade wing-chair, sat Alistair. I had remembered him as a giant, an unassailable colossus of familial authority; the man before me was shrunken, his frame lost in a woollen dressing gown, his face pale and drawn. Only his eyes were the same: chips of grey flint, cold and sharp.

He watched me approach without speaking. I stopped a few feet from his chair.

“You sent for me, Alistair,” I said.

“So I did,” he answered, his voice a rasp. “You took your time in coming. I trust your new employers could spare you from your duties.”

The barb was meant to sting; it was meant to remind me of my dependent station, so unlike his own inherited ease. A year ago, my cheeks would have burned with shame. Now, I felt nothing but a vague pity for the man who had only his wealth with which to wound.

“I came as soon as I was able. You said it was a matter of urgency.”

“It is. The estate is in chaos. My health, as you can see, is not what it was. There are papers to be sorted, accounts to be settled. A man in my position requires assistance.”

I looked at him then, truly looked into that proud, unyielding face, and I understood. He had not summoned me for reconciliation; he had not called me to his side to heal the wounds of a fractured childhood. He had summoned a clerk, an unpaid secretary whose familial bond he could exploit. The hope for amity, a foolish and feeble hope I had scarcely dared to acknowledge, died within me. It did not die a painful death, however; it simply expired, like a candle flame in a sudden draught. And in its place, a calm, hard certainty settled.

“And you believe I am the person for that work?” I asked.

“You can read, can you not? And write a fair hand? It is more than most of the village idiots I am forced to employ can manage. You will have a roof over your head. It is a better offer than you are likely to receive elsewhere.”

There it was: the familiar arrogance, the casual cruelty that had defined him all my life. I saw his plan quite clearly: he would work me to the bone, finding fault in all I did, until his health returned; then he would cast me out again with a pittance and a sneer. Rage, hot and sudden, rose in my throat, but I swallowed it down. I would not give him the satisfaction of tears or temper. I would be his mistress in this small matter, in spite of his expectations.

“I see,” I said slowly. “I will consider your proposition, Alistair. But I will not be treated as a servant in my own father’s house. I require a proper room, not the attic chamber I last occupied. And I shall take my meals where I choose. My stay here will be on my terms, or it will not be at all. You may let me know your decision in the morning.”

I turned and walked to the door, my back straight, my heart hammering against my ribs not with fear, but with a strange, fierce joy. I did not look back to see the shock on his face; I could feel it across the room, a palpable thing. I had entered this house a girl returning to her cage; I would remain in it as its master’s equal.

My battle was not with them; it was with myself, and for myself.

“Oh, Miss Jane,” she whispered, coming to my side. “I am so sorry. I heard. It is a wicked, wicked thing.”

“It is done, Bessie,” I said, laying a hand on her arm. “There is no help for it now.”

The stern lines of her mouth and brow were slackened, the despotic power that had defined her utterly gone. She was no longer my tyrant, no longer my aunt; she was merely a dying woman, her life’s account, like Eliza’s ledgers, soon to be closed.

“Will she wake again?” I asked.

“The doctor will say,” Bessie replied, shaking her head. “She has not spoken since before sunrise. I think… I think her mind is now too far gone.”

And so, it was over. There would be no final confrontation, no dramatic scene of accusation and confession. She had delivered her blow, and then she had retreated into the mists of approaching death, beyond my reach forever. I had vowed to be her mistress, to subdue her, but fate had denied me even that bitter satisfaction. There was nothing to subdue. There was only this husk, this remnant of a life filled with pride and hate.

I did not watch the figure on the bed. My gaze was fixed on the window, on the rain-streaked glass and the dreary park beyond. I thought of the letter, the tangible proof of my lost life, still lying in its hiding place. I thought of the fortune, now surely dispersed or inherited by others in some distant land. I thought of the man, John Eyre, who had died believing his niece had preceded him to the grave.

A strange peace began to settle over me. It was not the peace of forgiveness, for I had not forgiven her. It was the peace of finality. The long war of my childhood was, at last, truly over. The enemy was vanquished, not by any action of my own, but by the inexorable march of time and mortality. The anger, the grief, the burning sense of injustice—they were all still there, but they were no longer a tempest. They were hardening, solidifying into a foundation.

I was free. Not because I had received an apology, or because justice had been served, but because the source of my deepest pain was dissolving before my eyes. Her power over me had resided not in her actions, but in my reaction to them: in the hope of her approval, the fear of her displeasure, the longing for a reconciliation that could never be. Now, all that was gone. I had no more to hope or fear from her.

The doctor arrived, a portly, solemn man who went about his examination with a professional gravity. He spoke in low tones to Eliza, who had appeared at his side. I caught fragments: “a matter of hours,” “no more to be done,” “a peaceful end.” Georgiana, her face pale and swollen with weeping, hovered in the doorway, wringing a lace-trimmed handkerchief. She shot me a look of mingled fear and resentment, as if my very presence were an accusation.

I paid them no mind. My place was here, by this bed. I was not a mourner; I was a witness. I would see this through to the end, not for her sake, but for mine. It was the final chapter of the book of my servitude, and I would not leave until I had read the last word.

I remained in the chair all through that long day. Bessie brought me tea and a piece of bread, which I took mechanically. Eliza came and went, her efficiency a shield against emotion. Georgiana retired to her room with a bottle of smelling salts. The rain ceased, and a weak afternoon sun broke through the clouds, sending a single shaft of light into the dim, hushed room. It fell across the bed, illuminating the still, pale face of the woman who had blighted my youth. I looked at her then, truly looked, and felt nothing but a vast, empty calm. The hate was gone, replaced by a profound and desolate pity for a life so utterly wasted in bitterness.

As dusk began to gather once more in the corners of the room, her breathing changed. It became a series of shallow, rattling gasps, with long, silent pauses in between. Bessie, who had been sitting with her own sewing in a corner, put down her work and came to stand by my side. Eliza was summoned. She stood at the foot of the bed, her arms crossed, her face a rigid mask. Georgiana, alerted by a maid, crept in and collapsed into the armchair, her sobs muffled in her handkerchief.

There was a final, shuddering sigh. And then, silence. A silence more absolute and profound than any I had ever known.

The doctor, who had been waiting downstairs, was called. He made his brief, final confirmation. Mrs. Reed was dead.

Georgiana’s sobs devolved into loud hysterics. Eliza, her composure cracking for the first and only time, turned abruptly and stared out of the window, her back to the room. Bessie wept quietly into her apron. And I, Jane Eyre, sat motionless, my hands folded in my lap. I had shed my last tear for this woman long ago.

I rose from the chair. The vigil was over. I had seen what I came to see. I had entered this house seeking a reckoning and had found a ruin. I had returned expecting to fight an old battle and had instead borne witness to a quiet, pathetic surrender. I walked to the bed and looked down one last time at the face of my aunt. The lines of pride and despotism were gone, smoothed away by the impartial hand of death. She looked merely like an old, tired woman. I felt no triumph, no sorrow, no anger. I felt nothing at all. It was finished.

Without a word to my cousins, I left the chamber of death and went to the room that had been prepared for me. I had work to do. My life at Gateshead was over. My life in the world, the one I had to make for myself, was waiting. The knowledge of my lost inheritance did not embitter me; it liberated me. I owed no one anything. I was my own mistress, my own benefactor, the sole heir to the fortune of my own resilience. I would leave this house of ghosts on the morrow and never, ever return.

I had been told I was a burden, a dependent, a creature of a lower order; I had been made to feel my poverty and my orphan state as a crime. I had survived the red-room; I had survived Lowood; I had survived the desolation of my own heart. I would survive this too. The knowledge of what I had lost would not be a weight to drag me down; it would be a weapon. It was the final, incontrovertible proof that I owed these people nothing: not forgiveness, not pity, not one more moment of subservience to their whims.

I had come to see a dying aunt; I would remain to witness the end of an era. I would not seek the letter; its contents were already burned into my mind. Let it lie in her dressing-case, a hidden monument to her sin.

Her sorrows were great, but they were no longer my own. I had outgrown them.

I would meet whatever came next not as Jane Eyre the poor orphan, but as the woman who had been wronged and had endured. The enemy was vanquished, not by any action of my own, but by the inexorable march of time and mortality. The anger, the grief, the burning sense of injustice, they were all still there, but they were no longer a tempest. They were hardening, solidifying into a foundation.

“Yes,” I said. “I will marry you.”
